frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Credential-access tooling on scranton (Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil) plus LSASS access.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: LSASS opened with full-access rights (0x1f3fff/0x1fffff) by PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua; consistent with LSASS memory credential dumping.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_ALIAS handle requests on scranton were all made by lsass.exe itself as the machine account; no reg save or hive-copy of SAM observed.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No NTDS.dit file creation, ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines, or shadow-copy activity found (checks C025-C030 zero hits).

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No LSA Secrets / SECURITY Policy Secrets object access or lsadump/reg save HKLM\SECURITY command lines found (checks C032-C037 zero hits).

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: lsass.exe wrote HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua (4x) and scranton (1x), cached domain credential entry.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No DCSync/drsuapi/lsadump command lines or PowerShell script blocks found (checks C047/C048 zero hits).

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is the legitimate Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe -> netsh trace start/stop capture=yes to an .etl file, plus logman ETW sessions) on scranton.dmevals.local. No sniffing tools (tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap), no pcap/npcap/winpcap/ndis driver loads, no pcap/sniff/promiscuous command lines, and no ICMP conn records were found. The suspicious PsExec/sdelete activity observed is credential-access/lateral-movement, not network sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: LSASS handle requests observed; most are benign system/AV access (0x1000), but PowerShell full-access opens on scranton are suspicious.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: Get-Keystrokes keylogger and Get-Clipboard capture run by pbeesly on scranton.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No credential-prompt / GUI input capture artifacts found.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No IIS/wwwroot/login-portal capture activity in any dataset.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell opened LSASS with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on scranton; obfuscated PowerShell with GetProcAddress/UnsafeNativeMethods per anchors.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: No failed-logon (4625) events, lockouts, or brute-force patterns in any dataset; only benign RDP/CEIP logon notifications and normal 4648 explicit-credential logons.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: Zero 4625 failures and no repeated authentication attempts against any account; 'failed' message hits were unrelated system errors.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: LSASS accessed with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1fffff) by PowerShell on scranton.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625 failures and no single-source many-account authentication pattern; 4648 logons are legitimate PSEXESVC and machine-account logons.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons or credential-list-driven authentication attempts; credential material found is used for outbound WebDAV exfiltration, not stuffing.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA-interception artifacts exist in the data. The credential-flavored hits are benign: 4648 explicit-credential logons for pbeesly via PSEXESVC.exe/svchost.exe (PsExec lateral movement), LogonType 10 RDP logons using the Negotiate package (no smart-card/PKINIT/MFA provider), built-in CredentialEnrollmentManager service registration and a Credential Guard 'Enabled=0' registry write by lsass.exe, and a benign 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' message. Targeted hunts for smartcard/scard/MFA/token/vault/credential-provider processes, files, registry and PowerShell script blocks returned zero hits.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Zeek HTTP logs show host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) using DavClnt and Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 to reach 192.168.0.4 over WebDAV after SMB 445/139 attempts were rejected (REJ); the first PROPFIND carried an AUTHORIZATION header and the server returned 401 on /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z, consistent with forced authentication / NTLM credential capture.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: LSASS accessed with full access by PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: All T1539 hits have benign explanations: the 'cookie' command-line matches are WebDAV DavSetCookie (davclnt.dll) invocations by rundll32.exe on scranton.dmevals.local, and the only *cookie* file creation is an INetCookies artifact under the LocalService WARP JIT package profile created by svchost.exe. No browser cookie store (Chrome/Edge/Firefox Cookies, Login Data, Web Data) was created or accessed in Sysmon, Security or PowerShell data, no cookie-stealer tooling or PowerShell cookie references were found, and the Zeek HTTP GETs are WebDAV python.exe retrieval with no Cookie header. No evidence of web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Credential-harvesting toolkit (keystrokes, clipboard, screenshots) staged in SysinternalsSuite on scranton.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Hardcoded credentials in Invoke-Exfil script (cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd!) and PsExec command line (Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by).

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: Registry Password/Credential value sets were written by legitimate system processes (svchost, lsass, services, winlogon).

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No consolehost_history or shell-history access events found in sysmon/security.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificates to .pfx (coyn5igj.3io.pfx) on scranton.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: GptTmpl.inf/SecEdit access was routine Group Policy processing by svchost.exe and domain machines; no Groups.xml/cpassword access.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: PowerShell and WinRM host processes opened LSASS with full-access rights (credential dumping).

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: All browser-credential checks (Login Data, logins.json, cookies) returned zero hits across sysmon, security, powershell and other datasets.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: LSASS full-access handles consistent with Windows Credential Manager / DPAPI secret harvesting.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: All password-manager checks (KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass) returned zero hits across all datasets.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: LSASS accessed with full access rights by PowerShell on scranton (credential theft).

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: Network logons are machine-account (NEWYORK$ etc.) activity; no DC authentication backdoor (Skeleton Key/DSRM/auth-package tampering) observed.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password filter DLL registration or load artifacts in any dataset.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No reversible-encryption indicators (4739, Set-ADUser/dsmod, AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption) found.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No MFA configuration modification events (4739/5136) found.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No hybrid identity / federation modification events (5136, Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD) found.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No network provider DLL registration or modification artifacts found.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM positioning: object-access events are routine process/registry activity, Sysmon network connections all go to internal DC/host IPs on standard ports with no rogue destinations.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: SMB/Kerberos flows are legitimate pbeesly domain authentication to the DC; DNS queries are benign; no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning, no rogue SMB responder, no relay.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Each source MAC maps to a single source IP; the responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic dataset placeholder for the DC, not a MAC claiming multiple victim IPs. No gratuitous ARP.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP event codes in windows.other, no DHCP log type in Zeek, and no Sysmon traffic to ports 67/68.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: LSASS memory access by PowerShell and WinRM host on scranton/nashua (credential theft precursor).

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: All 4769 tickets used RC4 0x12 with normal ticket options; no forged-TGT or krbtgt-hash-theft-then-forge indicators found.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: Service tickets observed are KDC-issued for legitimate host SPNs with standard options; no silver-ticket indicators.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: Kerberos TGS requests for krbtgt and host SPNs by pbeesly (RC4) per anchors.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: No AS-REP roasting tooling or anomalous AS request patterns observed; PowerShell checks for AS-REP/GetNPUsers returned zero hits.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential artifacts. Logon-process stacking shows only normal Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp; windows.other 5857/5858 hits are routine WMI RSOP DeleteInstance by SYSTEM; zeek http/ssl/kerberos hits are WebDAV file transfers (OfficeSupplies.7z), not web auth.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie-related event is a benign INetCookies file creation by svchost.exe in a Windows service profile on scranton.dmevals.local. No PowerShell cookie/Set-Cookie/session script blocks (C344 zero hits) and no cookie-bearing HTTP auth traffic.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for SAML/NotOnOrAfter/Assertion in PowerShell (C348), saml/token/cert in Sysmon command lines (C350), and saml/adfs/token URLs in zeek HTTP (C351). No token-minting tooling or federated-service authentication observed.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA request generation activity in any dataset. The windows.other 5857/5858 hits are benign WMI/RSOP Group Policy processing by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on newyork.dmevals.local. Searches for MFA/2FA/authenticator/OTP/push-notification content in PowerShell 4104 script blocks (q-f6c2f78c1d, q-f33575842c), MFA/auth/login command lines in sysmon process creation (q-5f227202b6), and login/auth/MFA URLs in zeek HTTP (q-0bf9c8126b) all returned no matching events. Only one failed logon (4625) exists in the window, so there is no authentication-attempt flood. Note: unrelated credential-access-adjacent attacker activity (screen capture, 7Zip exfiltration by user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local) was observed but is not T1621.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on scranton.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

findings.title: Adversary credential-access tooling on scranton (pbeesly) — exfil staging script and LSASS access
findings.summary: The pbeesly account on scranton.dmevals.local ran a PowerShell script block 'Invoke-Exfil' (ScriptBlock ID b2b03a9c-43f0-4285-837d-f22d4600b2ae, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) that compresses user files with a password and copies them to a WebDAV share at \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials (cozy / MyCozyPassw0rd!). The same account's PowerShell activity includes file-collection targeting *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn* files. Combined with the LSASS full-access opens by PowerShell on the same host, this is consistent with an adversary performing credential access and collection.

findings.title: PowerShell and PowerShell Remoting processes opened LSASS with full memory-read access on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.623Z and 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16.654Z — full access masks that include 'Read from process memory', the classic LSASS-dump signature. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the PowerShell Remoting host) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29.430Z, and its CallTrace shows the PowerShell Commands.Management native image, indicating a PowerShell-based tool performing the access. Windows Security 4656 on scranton shows the pbeesly account via powershell.exe requesting AccessMask 0x1F3FFF on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. This is consistent with an adversary dumping LSASS memory for credential theft.

findings.title: Keystroke logging (Get-Keystrokes) and clipboard capture on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran Get-Keystrokes (PowerSploit/Empire keylogger that logs keys, time and active window) as a background job, and separately ran Get-Clipboard to capture clipboard contents. These are input-capture credential-theft actions not covered by the anchors.

The matching Security 4656 event shows pbeesly's powershell requesting AccessMask 0x1F3FFF on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. findings.summary: At 2020-05-02T03:21:29Z on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed an obfuscated PowerShell script block (function 'jzI' with random parameter names) that resolves Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods and calls GetProcAddress via reflection — a technique used to dynamically resolve and invoke native APIs (e.g. for hooking/credential access) while evading static detection. The same session also ran a gzip+base64 encoded scriptblock launched via a hidden powershell process, and 'Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas' for elevation.

LSASS memory accessed with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by steganographic PowerShell payload on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, IntegrityLevel High) was launched by control.exe with '-noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden' and executed a steganographic payload that decodes bytes from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX's them. The same process (SourceProcessId 2976) then opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff at 03:05:16Z — the classic signature of in-memory credential dumping (e.g. MiniDumpWriteDump) to obtain password hashes for offline cracking. This is attacker credential-access tooling, not brute force.

findings.summary: On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:14 and 00:32:21 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on ports 445 and 139; every attempt was rejected (conn_state REJ, 0 bytes), showing the target does not run SMB. The client then fell back to WebDAV over HTTP port 80: a DavClnt OPTIONS to '/' returned 403, followed by Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 OPTIONS and PROPFIND requests to /webdav, /webdav/ and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The first PROPFIND request carried an AUTHORIZATION header (client_header_names includes AUTHORIZATION) and the server answered 401 Unauthorized on the OfficeSupplies.7z path, i.e. the victim's credentials were transmitted to the attacker-controlled WebDAV listener. This is the classic forced-authentication chain (SCF/URL file or UNC path pointing at a WebDAV share) used to capture NTLM hashes. The activity is confined to the zeek window (2020-04-30) which does not overlap the Windows host logs (2020-05-02).

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script (loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1 / psversion.ps1) defining Get-PrivateKeys, which enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and exports every certificate with a thumbprint to a randomly-named .pfx in the user's Downloads folder, protected by the hardcoded password "saribas". A resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx was created by powershell.exe. This is new file-level evidence of the certificate/private-key theft beyond the anchor.

On 2020-05-02, user pbeesly's PowerShell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local (03:05:16) and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local (03:09:29) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff — the access masks used to read LSASS memory and harvest credentials. The same activity is corroborated by Windows Security object-access auditing (4663/4656) on the lsass.exe object with AccessMask 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff by the same processes/users. This is not the routine 0x1000/0x1400 query access seen from svchost/services; it is deliberate full-access to the credential store.

The 4697 service installs are normal Windows user services plus PSEXESVC/javamtsup (execution/lateral-movement artifacts, not AiTM).

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning; MAC-to-IP mappings are consistent with the dataset's synthetic addressing
findings.summary: Zeek conn records show three source MACs (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) each mapping to a single source IP (10.0.1.6, 10.0.1.4, 10.0.1.4 respectively). The responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a well-known synthetic placeholder that answers for the DC/responder IPs (10.0.0.4, 192.168.0.4, 192.168.0.5) and 10.0.1.6 — a dataset artifact, not a single MAC claiming multiple victim IPs. No gratuitous ARP, no duplicate MAC-to-IP conflict indicating poisoning.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing; no DHCP events or DHCP traffic present in any dataset
findings.summary: No DHCP-related Windows event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063) exist in windows.other, and no DHCP log type exists in the Zeek capture (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/dpd/smb_files/weird/smb_mapping/notice/pe). Sysmon network connections (event.code 3) show no traffic to DHCP ports 67/68; destination ports are standard service ports (8443, 389, 88, 53, 135, 445, 443). No rogue DHCP server activity is observable.

findings.title: No golden-ticket forging evidence observed
findings.summary: All 28 Kerberos service-ticket requests (event 4769) on newyork.dmevals.local used TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (RC4) with normal TicketOptions (0x40810000/0x60810010); no anomalous encryption downgrade, no forged-ticket indicators, and no krbtgt hash theft followed by forged TGT use were observed. The krbtgt TGS requests are attributable to normal Kerberos/DC replication behaviour. No golden-ticket activity could be confirmed.

findings.title: No silver-ticket forging evidence observed
findings.summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests observed on newyork.dmevals.local are all KDC-issued tickets for legitimate host SPNs (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) with standard ticket options and RC4 encryption; no service tickets issued without KDC validation or other silver-ticket indicators were found. No silver-ticket activity could be confirmed.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting evidence observed
findings.summary: No AS-REP roasting indicators were found: no PowerShell script blocks referencing AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth (check C334 returned zero hits), and no anomalous Kerberos AS request patterns were observed in the available data. No AS-REP roasting activity could be confirmed.

findings.title: No forged web credential activity; hits are LSASS access, WMI/RSOP noise and WebDAV file transfer
findings.summary: The T1606 check hits do not show any forging of web credentials. The windows.security logon-process stacking (312 events, q-60c287f89b) shows only normal Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp logon processes. The windows.other 5857/5858 hits (q-a16b4e80c0) are routine WMI RSOP_ExtensionStatus DeleteInstance operations by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on newyork.dmevals.local. The zeek http/ssl/kerberos hits (q-3658c152ef) are WebDAV file transfers between 10.0.1.4 and 192.168.0.4 (OfficeSupplies.7z), not web authentication. The LSASS process-access hits (q-9904cadde9) are credential-dumping-adjacent (T1003) rather than web-credential forgery.

findings.title: No forged web cookies; only a benign INetCookies file creation by svchost
findings.summary: The only cookie-related file event in the whole window is a single Sysmon file-create of C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies on scranton.dmevals.local, created by C:\windows\System32\svchost.exe (q-356e4f54d6 / q-d357b4f041). This is a normal Windows service-profile cookie store path, not browser cookie theft or forgery. No PowerShell script blocks referencing cookies/Set-Cookie/session were found (C344 zero hits), and the zeek HTTP traffic contains no cookie-bearing authentication requests.

findings.title: No SAML token forgery; no SAML/ADFS/token artifacts in any dataset
findings.summary: No SAML token forging activity was observed. PowerShell script-block searches for SAML/NotOnOrAfter/Assertion returned zero hits (C348), Sysmon process-command-line searches for saml/token/cert returned zero hits (C350), and zeek HTTP searches for saml/adfs/token URLs returned zero hits (C351). The windows.other 7045/5857/5858 hits (q-97ba48eaa3) are the same routine WMI RSOP DeleteInstance operations by SYSTEM on newyork.dmevals.local, unrelated to token minting. The only notable PowerShell activity is an obfuscated reflective shellcode loader on scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly), which is code-execution tradecraft (T1055/T1620), not SAML token forgery.

findings.title: No MFA request generation activity observed; windows.other 5857/5858 hits are benign WMI/RSOP GPO activity
findings.summary: The T1621 hypothesis (adversary generating repeated MFA push/notification requests to fatigue a user) is not supported by any retrieved event. The windows.other hits that triggered the check are WMI event 5858 records on newyork.dmevals.local, all executed by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (ClientProcessId 1588) performing IWbemServices::DeleteInstance against Root\Rsop\Computer RSOP_ExtensionStatus objects — routine Group Policy Resultant Set of Policy processing, not authentication or MFA activity. No PowerShell script block (4104) contained MFA/2FA/authenticator/OTP/push-notification/phone content, no sysmon process creation had MFA/auth/login command lines, and no HTTP request to a login/auth/MFA URL appeared in zeek. Only a single failed logon (4625) exists in the whole window, so there is no flood of authentication attempts characteristic of MFA fatigue.

findings.title: Routine certificate store registry writes and Kerberos TGT requests (benign)
findings.summary: The certificate-related registry writes flagged by the checks are normal Windows certificate store maintenance: Sysmon Event 13 writes to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\...\Blob by lsass.exe, svchost.exe, taskhostw.exe and powershell.exe (AuthRoot, MY, Windows Live ID Token Issuer, Remote Desktop stores), and a single Security 4657 modification of the ROOT\Certificates\BE36A456... key by NASHUA$ via C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe. The 4657 WMI Autologger entries under ControlSet001\Control\WMI\Autologger are unrelated to certificates. The 14 Kerberos 4768 TGT requests (pbeesly, SCRANTON$) on newyork.dmevals.local are ordinary domain logons with standard RC4 ticket options 0x40810010 and status 0x0. The Zeek x509 subjects (rempel.group.net, conn.sons.info) are from a non-overlapping window and show no forged authentication certificates.

findings.title: No shell-history credential access observed
findings.summary: No events referencing consolehost_history or PowerShell history files were found in windows.sysmon or windows.security. Although the attacker used an interactive PowerShell session on scranton, no evidence of reading shell history for credentials was retrieved.

incidents.title: PowerShell and WinRM host processes opened LSASS with full memory-read access on scranton and nashua
incidents.rationale: All of these findings describe the same attacker action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) on scranton.dmevals.local and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1F3FFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z and 03:09:29Z respectively. Full-access handles to LSASS memory are the canonical signature of OS credential dumping from LSASS memory, so T1003.001 (LSASS Memory) is the best-fitting in-scope technique; the findings' alternate labels (T1056.004, T1110.002, T1212, T1555, T1556, T1558) are not supported by the observed action.

incidents.title: LSASS wrote cached domain credential entry HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua
incidents.rationale: lsass.exe on nashua.dmevals.local repeatedly set HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 between 03:11:40Z and 03:15:03Z. The SECURITY\Cache\NL$ keys hold cached domain credentials (DCC/DCC2 hashes), so this is best described as Cached Domain Credentials (T1003.005); the finding itself notes lsass legitimately updates this key on interactive logon, hence suspicious rather than malicious.

incidents.title: Keystroke logging (Get-Keystrokes) and clipboard capture on scranton
incidents.rationale: pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran Get-Keystrokes (a keylogger logging keys, time and active window) as a background job and separately ran Get-Clipboard. Capturing keystrokes is input capture for credential theft, best fitting T1056.001 (Keylogging).

incidents.title: Obfuscated PowerShell resolving native APIs via GetProcAddress/UnsafeNativeMethods on scranton
incidents.rationale: pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local executed an obfuscated PowerShell script block (function 'jzI') that resolves Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods and calls GetProcAddress via reflection to dynamically invoke native APIs. Dynamically resolving and invoking native APIs in this manner is consistent with credential API hooking, so T1056.004 is the best-fitting in-scope technique.

incidents.title: Credential-harvesting and exfiltration toolkit staged in SysinternalsSuite on scranton
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same pbeesly PowerShell toolkit on scranton.dmevals.local (psversion.ps1) containing Get-Keystrokes, Get-Clipboard, Invoke-ScreenCapture and Invoke-Exfil, which compresses user files and copies them to a WebDAV share. The credential-collection functions (keystrokes, clipboard) are unsecured credential collection from the host, best fitting T1552 (Unsecured Credentials); the exfiltration staging is part of the same action.

incidents.title: Hardcoded credentials in PowerShell scripts and PsExec command line on scranton
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same exposure: pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran PsExec64.exe four times passing the plaintext password (-p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to run C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on \\NASHUA, and the Invoke-Exfil script embeds hardcoded credentials ($UserName "cozy", $Password "MyCozyPassw0rd!") for a WebDAV share. Credentials embedded in scripts and command lines are credentials in files, best fitting T1552.001.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on scranton
incidents.rationale: All three findings describe the same action: pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran Get-PrivateKeys (masqueraded as readme.ps1/psversion.ps1), which recursively enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports every certificate with a private key to a randomly named .pfx under Downloads protected by the hardcoded password "saribas", producing C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx. This is direct private-key theft, best fitting T1552.004 (Private Keys).

incidents.title: LSASS full-access handles consistent with Windows Credential Manager / DPAPI secret harvesting
incidents.rationale: The 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff handles to lsass.exe opened by pbeesly's PowerShell.exe (scranton) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua) give read access to LSASS memory where Windows Credential Manager / DPAPI master-key material resides, and the same user ran Get-PrivateKeys. The finding notes no legitimate Credential Manager cmdlet activity was observed, so the best-fitting in-scope technique for harvesting Windows Credential Manager secrets is T1555.004, at medium confidence.

incidents.title: Kerberos TGS requests for krbtgt and host SPNs by pbeesly (RC4)
incidents.rationale: On newyork.dmevals.local, pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL requested Kerberos service tickets (4769) for the krbtgt service and repeatedly for host SPNs NEWYORK$/NASHUA$ with TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (RC4), and SCRANTON$ requested krbtgt TGS. RC4 TGS requests for krbtgt are consistent with Kerberoasting-style ticket requests, best fitting T1558.003; the finding notes krbtgt is not a typical Kerberoasting target, hence suspicious/medium.

incidents.title: PsExec with cleartext password and sdelete on scranton/nashua (not network sniffing)
incidents.rationale: The finding itself states the observed activity is PsExec64.exe run against \\NASHUA with a cleartext password spawning python.exe via PSEXESVC, plus sdelete64.exe wiping files — credential/lateral-movement activity, not packet sniffing, so it does not satisfy T1040. The best-fitting ATT&CK technique for the observed action is remote services (T1021), which is out of scope for this credential-access hypothesis.

context_out_of_scope.title: Screen capture (Invoke-ScreenCapture) writing .bmp files on scranton
context_out_of_scope.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran Invoke-ScreenCapture, a background job that repeatedly writes screenshots to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.bmp. A resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\gwq4xdwv.s5g.bmp was created by powershell.exe. This is screen-capture collection not covered by the anchors.

context_out_of_scope.title: Local collection and staging: Rar archive of user files on nashua, 7z staging on scranton
context_out_of_scope.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, the PsExec-delivered C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe payload (running as pbeesly) dropped C:\Windows\Temp\Rar.exe and used it to create a password-protected archive C:\Users\pbeesly\Desktop\working.zip from C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\working.zip. On scranton, PowerShell compressed the Downloads directory into C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\OfficeSupplies.7z. These are new local-collection/staging artifacts.

context_out_of_scope.title: Anti-forensic deletion of staged archives and tools with sdelete on scranton and nashua
context_out_of_scope.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell ran SysinternalsSuite\sdelete64.exe to securely delete the staged archive and downloaded tooling (C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\Draft.Zip, C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\SysinternalsSuite.zip, and the victim .scr). On nashua.dmevals.local, cmd.exe ran C:\Windows\Temp\sdelete64.exe to delete C:\Windows\Temp\Rar.exe and the working.zip archives. These are new file-deletion artifacts.

context_out_of_scope.title: Ingress of tooling: SysinternalsSuite.zip download and python.exe/Rar.exe dropped on nashua
context_out_of_scope.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell wrote C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\SysinternalsSuite.zip (tooling ingress). On nashua.dmevals.local, the PsExec-delivered C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe (a PyInstaller bundle, extracting python27.dll and _MEI29522 modules) dropped C:\Windows\Temp\Rar.exe. These are new tool-transfer artifacts.
